title: Your short video did not need a better ending. It needed a first sentence.
markdown:
# Your short video did not need a better ending. It needed a first sentence.

You have the clip ready. The light is fine, the cut is clean, and the useful part arrives around second seven. Then you watch the retention line fall before you get there.

That hurts because the usual advice is so vague. “Make a stronger hook” sounds sensible right up until you sit down to write one. Stronger how? Louder? More dramatic? More personal? Most creators do not need another reminder to be interesting. They need a way to turn a real subject into an opening a stranger can understand before their thumb keeps moving.

The first three seconds have one job: give the right viewer a reason to wait for the next sentence. They do not have to explain the whole video. In fact, trying to explain everything is one of the fastest ways to lose the moment.

## Why decent videos get swiped past

A weak opening often starts with the creator's process instead of the viewer's problem.

“Today I want to talk about email marketing” is accurate, but it asks for attention before offering a reason. “Your welcome email is probably introducing you too late” puts a costly possibility on the table immediately. The viewer can decide whether it applies to them.

The difference is not trickery. It is specificity.

A useful hook usually contains one of these tensions:

- A familiar problem named more precisely than the viewer has named it.
- A result that sounds useful, paired with enough detail to feel earned.
- A claim that challenges a habit, then promises an explanation.
- A direct callout to the person the video is for.

None of those require a fake number, a borrowed story, or the phrase “wait until the end.” If the video cannot pay off the opening, the opening is wrong.

## Start with the moment before the pain

The best raw material is rarely the topic itself. It is the small moment that made the topic matter.

If you sell handmade jewelry, “three packaging tips” is a topic. “The packaging mistake that makes a $60 gift look like it came from a warehouse” is a moment. If you teach fitness, “how to squat” is a topic. “If your knees cave in on the way up, stop copying this cue” is a moment.

Try writing down the scene in one plain sentence:

> A person does X, expects Y, and gets Z instead.

That sentence gives you material for several openings without forcing you to repeat the same one forever. You can lead with the unwanted result, the mistaken expectation, or the person most likely to recognize the scene.

For a video about pricing a freelance service, the raw sentence might be: “A designer sends a proposal, hears nothing, and assumes the price was too high.” From there:

- “Silence after a proposal does not always mean your price was too high.”
- “Freelance designers: your proposal may be doing the selling too late.”
- “I would fix this line before lowering your rate.”

Each version makes a different promise. The rest of the video should answer that promise quickly.

## Give the spoken line and the screen different jobs

Creators often write one hook and put it everywhere. That wastes half the opening.

Use the spoken line for movement: a claim, a warning, a turn. Use the on-screen text for the detail someone needs while watching without sound. They should agree, but they do not need to be identical.

For example:

Spoken: “Your product demo starts where most viewers have already left.”

On screen: “Move the payoff before the setup.”

The spoken line creates a little pressure. The text gives the viewer a clean idea to hold onto. Keep both short enough to read and say without rushing. If either one needs a second breath, it probably belongs later in the script.

## Write options before you choose one

The first hook you write is usually attached to the script you already imagined. That attachment makes it hard to see a better entrance.

Write five openings for the same video, but make them genuinely different. One can call out the audience. One can challenge a common move. One can lead with stakes. One can name an awkward result. One can begin with the strongest useful claim you can defend.

Then read them out loud at normal speed. The winner is not necessarily the cleverest line. It is the line that makes the next sentence feel necessary.

## A small hook check before you film

Before recording, test the opening against four questions.

1. Could the intended viewer recognize themselves in the first sentence?
2. Does the line create a specific question that the next few seconds answer?
3. Can the video deliver that answer without stretching it into a bait-and-switch?
4. Would the line still make sense with the sound off, once the on-screen text is visible?

If the answer to the third question is no, lower the claim. A short video earns trust one promise at a time. The strongest hook is not the broadest statement you can make. It is the most precise promise the video can keep.

You may still lose viewers. Some people were never going to care about the subject, and that is fine. The point is to stop losing the people who would have cared if they had reached second seven.
